title: The body is the zero point of the world
subtitle: Evicted from the flesh
author: Gigla Gonashvili
introduction: What is the difference between human and machine? Classically, embodiment has been a go-to answer. But as information itself becomes increasingly embodied, the tension between metal and flesh is heightening. What it means to be embodied at all is here brought into question by philosopher Gigla Gonashvili.
body:
We are increasingly viewing ourselves as patterns rather than bodily presence, signals rather than substance. It is as if we are being evicted from the flesh, teleported directly into the realm of an alien intelligence. Yet, the body retains its own strange powers, as was already recognized by the materialist logic of the Stoics.

In How We Became Posthuman, N. Katherine Hayles writes that, with the arrival of the first wave of cybernetics, “information loses its body.” With the contribution of figures such as Norbert Wiener and Claude Shannon, information is divorced from lived meaning and context, falling into feedback loops and binary digits (“bits,” as coined by Shannon). The focus shifts onto function: just as a thermostat adjusts itself according to the room temperature, so too does a human body regulate its temperature by sweating. Wiener famously defines cybernetics as “Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine.”

Consequently, information gets tied to patterns and probabilistic functions which have to resolve, or at the very least drastically reduce, uncertainty—the “noise” in communication. In this way, information acquires generality and universality; it can be transported and teleported anywhere. Bodies, too, get dematerialized: they start to linger in virtual spaces, as is abundantly present in the genre of science fiction. Invoking William Gibson’s Neuromancer, Hayles notes that the body becomes “data made flesh.”

It is not the greenness of a tree that substantiates itself in the world, but rather its greening that takes place, opens itself as a horizon, and creates a volatile state in which all the constituents (tree and green) encode and envelop each other.

Information liberates itself from a material substratum in order to establish and maintain its own ontological status, becoming a primary medium of communication. Curiously, we can discern a similar trend in Stoic philosophy, which holds a strongly materialist ontology (such as in Zeno of Citium and Chrysippus, 3rd century BCE). For them, the whole universe is comprised of bodies—not only of the usual material sort (a stone), but the soul, too, is a body (hot breath, pneuma), and even Reason and God are bodies: fine substances. Furthermore, only a body can act or be acted upon. There is no interaction except between bodies.

But there is a twist. Besides these through-and-through material things, there are also four immaterial things (asomata): time, place, void, and that which is relevant for us, the so-called “sayables” (lekta). The famous Stoic example is that of a knife cutting flesh. Even though all entities involved (knife, flesh) are material, there arises an immaterial predicate: “being cut.” This predicate is not a new body, but something that persists through change or merely subsists. The Stoics used the verb huphistasthai to denote this latter category and differentiate it from existence—Huparchein—which implies the power of a beginning (arché), of a principle that can produce an action, which can only be a body.

It is important to understand that for the Stoics, the incorporeal predicates are neither the Platonic Forms, which exist in a separate non-physical realm, nor the accidents of the Aristotelian Substance, which hierarchically subordinates all the qualities that enter into contact with it. Rather, this in-formation of bodies and their ensuing disembodiment takes place on a flat plane—on a surface. This point is highly emphasized by none other than Gilles Deleuze, who sees in the Stoic elaboration of the asomata an understanding of an event, which is not a noun (something substantive), but a verb, an action.

It is not the greenness of a tree that substantiates itself in the world, but rather its greening that takes place, opens itself as a horizon, and creates a volatile state in which all the constituents (tree and green) encode and envelop each other. What arises, consequently, is not a cause-effect relation but rather a quasi-causation, an event (information) as an effect of a surface. As Ronald Bogue aptly notes, “the knife and flesh intermingle in the self-causing development of the cosmic body of God.”

What happens to our notion of a body in an age in which LLMs, feeding on the immense data of human knowledge, start interacting with us, becoming embedded in our environments—an age in which AI seems to be the sea where all rivers flow? It is clear that our gaze is becoming more and more fixed on information, and we like to think of our human nature as primarily pattern recognition. But in this arena, we are obviously surpassed by LLMs. This is why we need to rethink embodiment, or even reimagine it.

The body places itself into being and is itself a place.

For the Stoics, the intermingling of bodies generates an incorporeal surface: a detachment that causes us to lose our material point of reference. This same logic is at work, though drastically intensified, in modern AI. Yuval Noah Harari defines AI as “Alien Intelligence”, implying that we no longer know exactly how an LLM operates and that we are losing track of it. Yet, the alien can also be understood as a more visceral intrusion. Think, for example, of Ridley Scott’s Alien, where the action takes place on the Nostromo, a commercial spaceship traversing immense distances of cosmic darkness. The crew has to deal with an intrusion: a xenomorph that violently ruptures a crew member’s body from within, and whose acid blood can dissolve even the floor—a hard material thing.

Modern AI is not a traditional technology; it is not something primarily handheld and manipulated. It seeks to lodge itself within our very interiority and might, precisely by this trait, displace our essence, making it dissolve. We are therefore confused about our place in the world.

In this regard, it is worth noting that modern brain research—and this ties together with the cybernetic turn mentioned above—presents the brain as, in fact, something different from a body. As Lisa Feldman Barrett writes in How Emotions Are Made, the brain is trapped in a dark, silent box. It must constantly interpret the state of its own body. Am I out of breath because my belt is too tight, or because I am experiencing social anxiety? Strangely enough, the distinction is not always easy to make. Barrett argues that the primary task of the brain is not merely to model the outer world but to model its own body.

This latter point is important because it shows us that, even from the informatic point of view (of a brain), the body is not a mere thing among other things. The body places itself into being and is itself a place. We might think of it even as a spaceship, enveloped by immense darkness and intruded upon from the very inside.

SUGGESTED READING The embodied self By Ron McClamrock

Embodiedness puts us in contact with something primordial. We see, for example, in various ancient mythologies, such as Tiamat in the Enuma Elish or Purusha in the Rig Veda, that the cosmos comes into being through the dismemberment and rearrangement of a primordial body (e.g., eyes becoming the sun and feet becoming the earth). This is none other than the em-bodi-ment of the world that takes place through violence and, furthermore, through a spatialization, whereby the points of orientation (earth, sky, celestial bodies) are arranged.

By a dialectical twist, just as encoded information can displace and precipitate us (human subjects) towards disembodiment, so too can the body, inasmuch as it arises through its very displacement, enclose information, with all its folds and recesses, and thus resist dissolution. This is its utopian potential. As Michel Foucault writes:

My body, in fact, is always elsewhere. It is tied to all the elsewheres of the world. And to tell the truth, it is elsewhere than in the world, because it is around it that things are arranged. […] The body is the zero point of the world. There, where paths and spaces come to meet, the body is nowhere. It is at the heart of the world, this small utopian kernel from which I dream, I speak, I proceed, I imagine, I perceive things in their place […]. My body is like the City of the Sun. It has no place, but it is from it that all possible places, real or utopian, emerge and radiate.

What will happen to the body, with its utopian potential, in the age of AI? It is fair to say that the answer to this question is a prolonged and collective effort, inasmuch as we will try to think anew the meaning of our embodiedness. In the meantime, it is certainly useful to keep in mind these potentialities of our bodies, since they can be, among other things, unsettling and dangerous. For example, a body might precipitate itself towards mythological phantasms and try to delusionally reinstate itself within a primordial, uncontaminated unity by purging parasites, or by protecting itself from the “alien intrusion.”

Does information have a body? Or rather, does it have an environment? For Hayles, what distinguishes the body from the disembodied nature of information is that it is grounded in the world, in the environment. Yet, modern AI suggests that information, too, can have an environment. For if a model (LLM) can learn, adapt, and rearrange its data, then it is embedded in reality. This raises the stakes. And, as is held in Stoic philosophy, if all that exists are bodies, this brings us—humans and the alien intelligence—into closer contact with each other, both metaphorically and literally.
